title: The root of character
hook: William James: the power to bring back a wandering attention again and again is the very root of judgment and will

segments.voice: Yesterday, monks in the lab: people who look at the mind from the inside, and people who measure it from the outside, at one table. Your line was monks and scientists. What question about your own mind did you carry? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

The bottom of the page arrives, and not one sentence of it stayed. The eyes went line by line. The mind went to the grocery list, an old argument, the dentist. So back up to the top and start again. Now, that moment of noticing, and turning back to the page, sounds like a small failure. A psychologist and philosopher named William James thought it was something else entirely. In his big textbook on the mind, in the chapter on attention, he named that little turn back as the root of something very large.
screen: `THE PAGE YOU DIDN'T READ.` → `THE TURN BACK.` → `A ROOT, NOT A FAILURE.`

segments.voice: Here are William James's words, from The Principles of Psychology: "the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." Look at what he didn't say. He didn't say the root of character is never wandering. He takes wandering for granted. The faculty he prizes is the return, over and over again, and voluntarily: you choose it. So every drift is not the end of practice. It's the raw material. No drift, no return. Then he adds a Latin phrase: "No one is compos sui if he have it not." Compos sui means master of oneself. Without the power to come back, James says, nobody is quite in charge of their own life. Judgment, character, will: the big words all grow from this small, repeated act. And then comes an honest admission. He says an education that improved this faculty would be the education par excellence, and then admits: "it is easier to define this ideal than to give practical directions for bringing it about." The author of a whole textbook on the mind, saying plainly: I can tell you what matters, but I can't tell you how to train it. That's the open question this part of the path keeps asking. Some contemplative traditions offer a method: sit, notice the drift, return. Science asks whether that method actually changes anything. Today, just start where James started: with the turn back.
screen: `THE FACULTY OF BRINGING IT BACK.` · `EVERY DRIFT IS RAW MATERIAL.` · `COMPOS SUI: MASTER OF ONESELF.` · `EASIER TO DEFINE THAN TO TRAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring your attention back ten times. Settle, and choose the breath as home: the air at the nostrils, or the rise of the belly. Rest there. Sooner or later the mind will wander. When you notice, silently count one, and come back to the breath. Next time you notice, two. Don't scold the drift; each one is a chance to practice the turn. See if you reach ten before the bell. If you reach it early, keep going. The bell holds the time.
The root of character. William James's name for the power to bring a wandering attention back, over and over again. Today's word.

Your line: bring it back. Today, each time you catch your mind elsewhere in the middle of a conversation or a task, don't sigh. Count it as one more turn, and bring it back. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: In breath-focused meditation, practitioners rest attention on the breath and, each time they notice it has wandered, gently return it; teachers often describe each return, not the stillness, as the actual exercise.

fork.setup: your mind has wandered off the page for the third time in a minute. by William James's account, what's the faculty that matters here?
options: never letting the mind wander at all.
bringing it back, voluntarily, over and over.
forcing the mind to stay by sheer effort.
fork.reveal: "the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." the wandering is assumed. the return is the root.

original.note: Latin, used by William James: master of oneself, in possession of oneself.

trapdoor: what you thought: good attention means a mind that never drifts.
what it means: the drift is expected. what builds judgment and will is the return, chosen, over and over again.
what a scholar hears: the chapter on attention in The Principles of Psychology, where James calls an education in this faculty the education par excellence, then admits he can't say how to give it.
